How large rocket would be needed to send a spacecraft to Venus to collect samples and then return to Earth?

At a guess : insanely large.
You'd need to build a rocket large enough to lift another rocket, each able to also go fast enough to do the trip.

The second rocket would also need to be durable enough to survive Venus' hellish conditions. ( and I don't think rocket fuel is meant to be cooked )

So workign this backwards, The return system would be very small, using a solar electric propulsion system it would mass around two tons to get home from Venus, much of which would be the reentry system+sample. Since we're moving in, we have a LOT of power to work with, a simple ion engine would require just 15% of its mass to be fuel to come home. Overall it doesn't effect the total mass of the system, because it's not going to land, it'll take the sample away from the launch vehicle in orbit, because every kilogram involved in getting OFF of venus will be a nightmare.

So next up, we need a launch vehicle... this is the really amazingly hard part. So we're going to use a methane fuel system (I'll get to why later), and we need a total of 27km/s of deltaV for the orbit (sourced from the real solar system mod for Kerbal Space Program where you can actually try to launch off venus if you're insane). As it turns out we know exactly the booster for this, because that's about what New Horizon launched with. You need an all methane atlas V Those boosters need to be bigger, since they're methane, and methane isn't as efficient as hydrogen so you need more fuel, but that mostly means bigger boosters, methane is also denser so the fuel tank won't be any bigger). The engines will have to be designed from the ground up, some back of the envelope math says you can in fact get off the ground at 92 atmospheres, but no engine we've ever built is capable, the efficiency isn't even that bad, if you design for it, (the SRB is a wash, though). For all this you're putting around 400 kilograms into orbit, not bringing it home, thus the small electric propulsion vehicle to take it the rest of the way.

Now about that atlas... it masses 566 tons, fully fueled (not including our miniscule payload). That's be 5 SLS block II (which will be the largest rocket ever built) launches just to get it into orbit! But it only weighs abouy 50 tons empty. An ampty rocket doesn't do us much good, but the atmosphere of venus is mostly carbon dioxide, this was alreaydy worked out for mars, bring hydrogen, mix with carbon dioxide, get methane, and oxygen. this saves 97% of the fuel mass. Now it's just 65 tons. Add some mass for a landing system, but, at the end of the day you could launch this whoel system all the way to venus... on a single SLS block II, since the system is a lot less than the 130 ton orbital capability it'll easily boost it the rest of the way to venus.

There are some technical problems here, like venus is going try and melt the rocket, not to mention boil all the fuel. I'm honestly not sure that these could be solved. But if they can be solved, that's you answer, the entire thing happens on a single SLS launch, you can even hitch the return system along for the ride, assuming it has enough fuel to brake in orbit (the landing vehicle will just land, using venus's atmosphere to slow itself down).

This doesn't include the finanical cost to invent all the shit I just described either, 100 billion would be a bargain.

A sample return mission would not be set up in a single spacecraft. Aside from the obvious complications due to the extremes in environments and variety of tasks, you're looking at wasteful energy use in several stages of the mission. You'd have to design the mission with several specialized spacecrafts.

The first would be, likely, several rockets to deliver the spacecrafts to Venus. This would be partially due to mass constraints but primarily that NASA would never get that kind of financial support from the government. It would be spread out over many, many years. Possibly 20-25.

(Scenario 1) I would hypothesize the tasks would be split up as such:
Lander
Lander assist
Sample Launch assist
Orbiter / Return craft
Capture craft

Lander
Think of the Curiosity mission and how complex it was to land something approximately the size of an SUV. You'll probably need something around the same size and weight to land and move around the surface under its own power. It'll have to be able to communicate at least up to the Orbiter to communicate with Earth. We would have to be able to communicate with it to maneuver and find the samples to be returned. The lander would also have to be built to withstand the extreme greenhouse effect heat of around 450 ºC (850 ºF), the atmospheric pressure 92 times the atmospheric pressure of Earth, and the heavy sulfuric acid content of the atmosphere.
Just as it was with Curiosity, a lander assist unit would be required for a safe touchdown. At the end of the collection stage of the mission, the lander would be left behind. There is no reason to attempt to lift the lander back into space that would not add excessive difficulty to the mission's success. The samples alone would need some kind of launch assist to get back to space. Chemical thrust rockets would likely be used but would not fare well at the surface temperatures and atmospheric pressure for the duration of the collection.

Lander Assist
As mentioned before, a lander of a desired size to move, collect and communicate under its own power would probably need some kind of landing assist to prevent excessive force in landing. Just like with the Curiosity mission, the lander assist would be abandoned once its task is complete. The denser atmosphere could be taken advantage of to allow other speed reduction methods.

Sample Launch Assist
The conditions on Venus are quite hostile and you'd want to limit the exposure of the rocket fuselage. A possibility off the top of my head is some kind of launch platform, in a similar but smaller architecture of a Russian ballistic missile launch vehicle to set down after the collection lander has finished its job. Obviously the sample launch platform would be much smaller since the payload is much smaller. Once it lands, the collection lander would rendezvous to transfer the samples quickly before lifting off. The mass requirements of the launch platform and rocket only need to get the sample into orbit, not all the way back to Earth.

Orbiter / Return
The main array for communications between Earth, itself and the lander could be housed in it to prevent the damage from exposure to Venus' atmosphere as well as the fuel required to return to Earth. It would also be equipped to capture the payload container from the sample launch assist.

Capture
This could be optional as it could be possible to design the orbiter for Earth atmosphere reentry. Once the orbiter returns to Earth with the samples there needs to be a way to get them safely to the surface. One option, as previously mentioned, the orbiter could be designed for Earth reentry and an ocean splash-down. Since the orbiter is also the main communications array it wouldn't be too hard to design in the ability to de-orbit on command and to activate a retrieval beacon. Otherwise, the orbiter would be told to adjust its speed and direction to orbit Earth with a retrieval mission launch.

(Scenario 2)
Instead of a mobile lander and lander assist, previous research could find possible locations of interest. Other methods than visual light would be required since we can't see the ground with the visible spectrum of light. Many sample launch units could land, collect samples from its landing location, and lift off all from the one unit. This would allow the vehicles to require less resistance to the hostile conditions of Venus. It would also allow for a larger margin of failure since all the samples won't be in one vehicle, the exposure window is much shorter and there are far fewer "moving parts". This would obviously require many more Venus destination rockets due to sheer volume.
As I think it through, "Scenario 2" is much more viable for mission success.
